context_blurb:
Many cliffs and quarries show rock in layers, piled like the pages of a book that Earth has been writing since its birth. Geologists, the scientists of Earth's rock, learned to read those pages: their order, how layers far apart match, and how long the whole story runs.

In 1669 the Danish scientist Nicolas Steno saw that layers of sand and mud settle one on another, so in an undisturbed stack each layer is younger than the one beneath it.

In the 1790s William Smith, an English canal surveyor, saw the same layers turn up again and again in mines and cuttings. Two sandy layers could look like twins, yet Smith could name each one. He went by its fossils, the remains of ancient living things kept in stone: each layer held fossils of its own, so it could be known by them wherever it showed, however much it thinned or thickened. His 1815 map of England and Wales was the first detailed geological map of a whole country; William Maclure's rougher map of the United States came out in 1809.

A fossil that links layers in distant lands, showing they formed at one time, is an index fossil. The best index fossil comes from a kind of creature that spread all over the world but lived for only a short span. Its spread links continents, and its short life pins the layers to a narrow slice of the past, while a long-lived kind turns up in rocks of many ages.

In 1788 the Scottish geologist James Hutton sailed to Siccar Point, where grey layers stand almost upright, their tops worn level, under red sandstone. Such a junction is an unconformity, a gap in the rock record. The grey layers had settled flat on an old sea floor, hardened, been tipped on end and worn down before any red sand arrived, and Hutton knew how slowly such work goes on today. So he concluded that Earth's history reaches back an immense time, far beyond the few thousand years many in his day allowed. In the rocks, he wrote, he found "no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end."

Hutton's reasoning rested on an assumption later named uniformitarianism: reading the past through the present. A geologist who finds ancient ripples in sandstone, shaped like those a stream leaves in sand today, reads them as the work of flowing water, trusting that the same natural laws worked in the past as now. That does not mean Earth's face never changed: seas and mountains came and went, and rare great events struck, all under the same laws.

Through the 1800s geologists built the geologic time scale, a calendar of Earth's past whose longest spans, eons, split into eras and then periods. Layers and fossils gave each span a relative age: its place in the order, older or younger than the rest. They could not give an absolute age, an age in years, so no one could say how many years ago any period began. A wall of layers is like a pile of undated letters: the order shows, but not when each was written. Dates in years came only in the 1900s.

The last three eras are named for their life: Paleozoic means old life, Mesozoic middle life and Cenozoic new life. Geologists drew the lines between them where the fossils suddenly change, and both lines mark mass extinctions, times when many kinds of living things died out together. The Paleozoic ended about 252 million years ago in the Great Dying, which took some nine in ten kinds of sea life; the Mesozoic ended about 66 million years ago with the last big dinosaurs.

In the 1800s Lord Kelvin, reckoning from how fast Earth cools, gave it 20 to 400 million years, far too few. Today geologists know that Earth formed, with the rest of the solar system, about 4.6 billion years ago, a third of the universe's age of 13.8 billion years.

Squeeze all 4.6 billion years into one day, from Earth's birth at midnight to now at the next midnight, and each second stands for about 53,000 years. The last big dinosaurs vanish some twenty minutes short of midnight, and the human line splits from the chimpanzees' about two minutes before the end. The first modern humans, who appeared about 300,000 years ago, arrive just a few seconds before midnight. No person ever saw a big dinosaur alive.
